claim: Dlx5/6-Cre mediated forebrain deletion of torsinA causes abnormal twisting in mice.
source: Previously (Pappas et al., 2015;4:e08352), we reported that Dlx5/6-Cre mediated forebrain deletion of the DYT1 dystonia protein torsinA (Dlx-CKO) causes abnormal twisting and selective degeneration of dorsal striatal cholinergic interneurons (ChI) (Pappas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Dlx5/6-Cre mediated forebrain deletion of torsinA causes selective degeneration of dorsal striatal cholinergic interneurons.
source: Previously (Pappas et al., 2015;4:e08352), we reported that Dlx5/6-Cre mediated forebrain deletion of the DYT1 dystonia protein torsinA (Dlx-CKO) causes abnormal twisting and selective degeneration of dorsal striatal cholinergic interneurons (ChI) (Pappas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: ChAT-CKO mice phenocopy the Dlx-CKO phenotype of selective dorsal striatal ChI loss.
source: ChAT-CKO mice phenocopy the Dlx-CKO phenotype of selective dorsal striatal ChI loss and identify an essential requirement for torsinA in brainstem and spinal cholinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ChI loss in ChAT-CKO mice.

claim: TorsinA is required for survival or function of brainstem cholinergic neurons.
source: ChAT-CKO mice phenocopy the Dlx-CKO phenotype of selective dorsal striatal ChI loss and identify an essential requirement for torsinA in brainstem and spinal cholinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced cholinergic neurons in brainstem nuclei of ChAT-CKO mice.

claim: TorsinA is required for survival or function of spinal cholinergic neurons.
source: ChAT-CKO mice phenocopy the Dlx-CKO phenotype of selective dorsal striatal ChI loss and identify an essential requirement for torsinA in brainstem and spinal cholinergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced motor neurons in spinal cord of ChAT-CKO mice.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice are tremulous.
source: ChAT-CKO mice are tremulous, weak, and exhibit trunk twisting and postural abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral observations described in the manuscript.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice are weak.
source: ChAT-CKO mice are tremulous, weak, and exhibit trunk twisting and postural abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing reduced latency to fall in forelimb suspension test.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit trunk twisting.
source: ChAT-CKO mice are tremulous, weak, and exhibit trunk twisting and postural abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral observations described in the manuscript.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit postural abnormalities.
source: ChAT-CKO mice are tremulous, weak, and exhibit trunk twisting and postural abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing severe kyphosis in ChAT-CKO mice.

claim: There is a cell autonomous requirement for torsinA in specific populations of cholinergic neurons.
source: These findings are the first to demonstrate a cell autonomous requirement for torsinA in specific populations of cholinergic neurons, strengthening the connection between torsinA, cholinergic dysfunction and dystonia pathophysiology.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing ChI loss in ChAT-CKO mice where torsinA is deleted specifically from cholinergic neurons.

claim: Striatal cholinergic dysfunction is implicated in dystonia pathophysiology.
source: Multiple lines of evidence implicate striatal cholinergic dysfunction in dystonia pathophysiology (Pappas et al., 2015; Albin et al., 2003; Eskow Jaunarajs et al., 2015; Pappas et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: DYT1 dystonia is caused by a loss of function mutation in the gene encoding torsinA.
source: The symptoms of DYT1 dystonia, caused by a loss of function mutation in the gene encoding torsinA (Ozelius et al., 1997), are reduced by antimuscarinic treatments (e.g., trihexyphenidyl)(Burke et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Ozelius et al., 1997).

claim: Symptoms of DYT1 dystonia are reduced by antimuscarinic treatments.
source: The symptoms of DYT1 dystonia, caused by a loss of function mutation in the gene encoding torsinA (Ozelius et al., 1997), are reduced by antimuscarinic treatments (e.g., trihexyphenidyl)(Burke et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Burke et al., 1986).

claim: Antimuscarinic agents reduce motor abnormalities in DYT1 mouse models.
source: Antimuscarinic agents also reduce motor (Pappas et al., 2015) and electrophysiological (Maltese et al., 2014) abnormalities in DYT1 mouse models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Antimuscarinic agents reduce electrophysiological abnormalities in DYT1 mouse models.
source: Antimuscarinic agents also reduce motor (Pappas et al., 2015) and electrophysiological (Maltese et al., 2014) abnormalities in DYT1 mouse models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Maltese et al., 2014).

claim: Striatal cholinergic dysfunction is a common feature of multiple DYT1 animal models.
source: Striatal cholinergic dysfunction is a common feature of multiple DYT1 animal models (Pappas et al., 2015; Martella et al., 2009; Pisani et al., 2006; Sciamanna et al., 2012a; Sciamanna et al., 2012b), and experimental ablation of striatal cholinergic interneurons (ChI) can lead to abnormal postures (Kaneko et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Experimental ablation of striatal cholinergic interneurons can lead to abnormal postures.
source: Striatal cholinergic dysfunction is a common feature of multiple DYT1 animal models (Pappas et al., 2015; Martella et al., 2009; Pisani et al., 2006; Sciamanna et al., 2012a; Sciamanna et al., 2012b), and experimental ablation of striatal cholinergic interneurons (ChI) can lead to abnormal postures (Kaneko et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Kaneko et al., 2000).

claim: Deletion of torsinA from forebrain GABAergic and cholinergic neurons causes highly selective degeneration of dorsal striatal ChI.
source: We demonstrated previously that deletion of torsinA from forebrain GABAergic and cholinergic neurons (using Dlx5/6-cre; 'Dlx-CKO') causes highly selective degeneration of dorsal striatal ChI roughly coincident with the juvenile onset of abnormal limb clasping and twisting movements(Pappas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Degeneration of dorsal striatal ChI in Dlx-CKO mice is roughly coincident with the juvenile onset of abnormal limb clasping and twisting movements.
source: We demonstrated previously that deletion of torsinA from forebrain GABAergic and cholinergic neurons (using Dlx5/6-cre; 'Dlx-CKO') causes highly selective degeneration of dorsal striatal ChI roughly coincident with the juvenile onset of abnormal limb clasping and twisting movements(Pappas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Selective ChI abnormalities are present in postmortem tissue from DYT1 subjects.
source: Selective ChI abnormalities are also present in postmortem tissue from DYT1 subjects (Pappas et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Abnormal movements in Dlx-CKO mice are reduced by clinically relevant antimuscarinic treatments.
source: Abnormal movements in Dlx-CKO mice are reduced by clinically relevant antimuscarinic treatments, strengthening model therapeutic validity and suggesting shared pathophysiology with human dystonia.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit approximately 34% reduction in the number of dorsal striatal ChI compared to control mice.
source: Unilateral unbiased stereology of ChAT-immunoreactive neurons in the dorsal striatum from 1 year old mice demonstrates a ~ 34% reduction in the number of dorsal striatal ChI in ChAT-CKO mice compared to control mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological quantification data presented in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Bilateral unbiased stereology confirms a 48% reduction in dorsal striatal ChI in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: This finding was confirmed in an independent cohort using bilateral unbiased stereology (48% reduction; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data from an independent cohort shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The number of striatal non-cholinergic neurons in ChAT-CKO mice is not different from controls.
source: The number of striatal non-cholinergic neurons was not different from controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), demonstrating that there are no secondary cell loss effects of ChI degeneration, and that torsinA loss of function-mediated neurodegeneration is highly specific.
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: There are no secondary cell loss effects of ChI degeneration in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: The number of striatal non-cholinergic neurons was not different from controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), demonstrating that there are no secondary cell loss effects of ChI degeneration, and that torsinA loss of function-mediated neurodegeneration is highly specific.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no change in non-cholinergic neuron numbers.

claim: TorsinA loss of function-mediated neurodegeneration is highly specific.
source: The number of striatal non-cholinergic neurons was not different from controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C), demonstrating that there are no secondary cell loss effects of ChI degeneration, and that torsinA loss of function-mediated neurodegeneration is highly specific.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing selective loss of cholinergic neurons without loss of other neuron types.

claim: ChI cell loss in Dlx-CKO mice occurs primarily in the dorsal aspects of the striatum.
source: ChI cell loss is strikingly selective in Dlx-CKO mice, occurring primarily in the dorsal aspects of the striatum, with approximately six times greater cell loss in the dorsolateral compared to ventromedial striatum (57% vs 9% cell density reduction in Dlx-CKO mice; [Pappas et al., 2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit approximately six times greater cell loss in the dorsolateral compared to ventromedial striatum.
source: ChI cell loss is strikingly selective in Dlx-CKO mice, occurring primarily in the dorsal aspects of the striatum, with approximately six times greater cell loss in the dorsolateral compared to ventromedial striatum (57% vs 9% cell density reduction in Dlx-CKO mice; [Pappas et al., 2015]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Pappas et al., 2015).

claim: Significant reductions in ChI number in ChAT-CKO mice are limited to the dorsolateral and dorsomedial segments of the dorsal striatum.
source: Significant reductions in ChI number were limited to the dorsolateral and dorsomedial segments of the dorsal striatum (72% and 54% cell density reductions in dorsolateral and dorsomedial, vs 12% and −4% in ventrolateral and ventromedial segments; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell density data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit 72% cell density reduction in dorsolateral striatum.
source: Significant reductions in ChI number were limited to the dorsolateral and dorsomedial segments of the dorsal striatum (72% and 54% cell density reductions in dorsolateral and dorsomedial, vs 12% and −4% in ventrolateral and ventromedial segments; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell density data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit 54% cell density reduction in dorsomedial striatum.
source: Significant reductions in ChI number were limited to the dorsolateral and dorsomedial segments of the dorsal striatum (72% and 54% cell density reductions in dorsolateral and dorsomedial, vs 12% and −4% in ventrolateral and ventromedial segments; Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell density data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The topographic pattern of ChI cell loss in ChAT-CKO mice is present throughout the entire rostro-caudal extent of the striatum.
source: This topographic pattern of cell loss was present throughout the entire rostro-caudal extent of the striatum (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The dorsolateral striatum is a key motor circuit node functionally integrated according to topographic inputs.
source: The dorsolateral selectivity of ChI neuron loss is highly relevant, as the dorsolateral striatum is a key motor circuit node functionally integrated according to topographic inputs, whereas ventromedial striatal neurons are connected in associative and limbic circuits (Alexander et al., 1986; Haber, 2016; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Alexander et al., 1986; Haber, 2016; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).

claim: Ventromedial striatal neurons are connected in associative and limbic circuits.
source: The dorsolateral selectivity of ChI neuron loss is highly relevant, as the dorsolateral striatum is a key motor circuit node functionally integrated according to topographic inputs, whereas ventromedial striatal neurons are connected in associative and limbic circuits (Alexander et al., 1986; Haber, 2016; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Alexander et al., 1986; Haber, 2016; Parent and Hazrati, 1995).

claim: The basal forebrain contains cholinergic projection neurons subserving cognitive and attentional control.
source: In contrast, the basal forebrain contains cholinergic projection neurons subserving cognitive and attentional control (Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Ballinger et al., 2016), which do not degenerate in either model (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Ballinger et al., 2016).

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons do not degenerate in Dlx-CKO or ChAT-CKO mice.
source: In contrast, the basal forebrain contains cholinergic projection neurons subserving cognitive and attentional control (Hasselmo and Sarter, 2011; Ballinger et al., 2016), which do not degenerate in either model (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Conditional deletion of torsinA from forebrain cholinergic neurons mimics the region-selective vulnerability observed in Dlx-CKO mice.
source: Conditional deletion of torsinA from forebrain cholinergic neurons therefore mimics the region-selective vulnerability observed in Dlx-CKO mice, demonstrating a cell autonomous requirement for torsinA in select cholinergic populations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of ChAT-CKO and Dlx-CKO phenotypes.

claim: TorsinA levels are reduced to a greater extent in ventral ChI compared to dorsal ChI at P0 in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: Surprisingly, despite uniform prenatal Cre recombinase expression and preferential loss of dorsal ChI, torsinA levels were reduced to a greater extent in ventral ChI (dorsal ChI contained 82% of control torsinA levels, while ventral ChI had ~52% remaining; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by torsinA immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Dorsal ChI in ChAT-CKO mice contain 82% of control torsinA levels at P0.
source: Surprisingly, despite uniform prenatal Cre recombinase expression and preferential loss of dorsal ChI, torsinA levels were reduced to a greater extent in ventral ChI (dorsal ChI contained 82% of control torsinA levels, while ventral ChI had ~52% remaining; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by torsinA immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Ventral ChI in ChAT-CKO mice contain approximately 52% of control torsinA levels at P0.
source: Surprisingly, despite uniform prenatal Cre recombinase expression and preferential loss of dorsal ChI, torsinA levels were reduced to a greater extent in ventral ChI (dorsal ChI contained 82% of control torsinA levels, while ventral ChI had ~52% remaining; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by torsinA immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Non-vulnerable basal forebrain cholinergic neurons exhibit 49% of control torsinA immunoreactivity at P0 in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: Non-vulnerable basal forebrain cholinergic neurons exhibited 49% of control torsinA immunoreactivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by torsinA immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: A more rapid loss of torsinA during development does not contribute to the unique vulnerability of dorsal ChI.
source: These findings demonstrate that a more rapid loss of torsinA during development does not contribute to the unique vulnerability of dorsal ChI.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that vulnerable dorsal ChI retain more torsinA than non-vulnerable ventral ChI and basal forebrain neurons.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice have significantly fewer cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus compared to controls.
source: Unbiased stereology of ChAT-immunoreactive neurons in the brainstem demonstrates significantly fewer cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine (PPN) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) nuclei in 1 year old Chat-CKO mice (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice have significantly fewer cholinergic neurons in the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus compared to controls.
source: Unbiased stereology of ChAT-immunoreactive neurons in the brainstem demonstrates significantly fewer cholinergic neurons in the pedunculopontine (PPN) and laterodorsal tegmental (LDT) nuclei in 1 year old Chat-CKO mice (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The PPN and LDT contain GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in addition to cholinergic neurons.
source: The PPN and LDT also contain GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons (Mena-Segovia, 2016), which significantly outnumber cholinergic neurons (Mena-Segovia et al., 2009; Wang and Morales, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Mena-Segovia et al., 2009; Wang and Morales, 2009).

claim: GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons significantly outnumber cholinergic neurons in the PPN and LDT.
source: The PPN and LDT also contain GABAergic, and glutamatergic neurons (Mena-Segovia, 2016), which significantly outnumber cholinergic neurons (Mena-Segovia et al., 2009; Wang and Morales, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia et al., 2009; Wang and Morales, 2009).

claim: Unbiased stereology of NeuN+ neurons in PPN and LDT showed no significant change in the overall number of neurons in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: Unbiased stereology of NeuN +neurons in PPN and LDT showed no significant change in the overall number of neurons (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by stereological data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: The loss or dysfunction of brainstem cholinergic neurons does not have deleterious effects on the viability of surrounding neurons in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: These findings also indicate that the loss or dysfunction of brainstem cholinergic neurons does not have deleterious effects on the viability of surrounding neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing no change in overall NeuN+ neuron numbers despite loss of cholinergic neurons.

claim: There is no evidence of reactive microgliosis or astrogliosis in the brainstem of ChAT-CKO mice.
source: Consistent with this finding, there was no evidence of reactive microgliosis or astrogliosis in the brainstem (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice have significantly fewer spinal motor neurons (C3-C5) compared to controls.
source: Quantification of the number of spinal motor neurons (C3-C5; [Kim et al., 2017]) demonstrated significantly fewer motor neurons in ChAT-CKO mice (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons are distributed in a rostrocaudal continuum in the brainstem, forming a coordinated functional unit.
source: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons are distributed in a rostrocaudal continuum in the brainstem, forming a coordinated functional unit (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Mena-Segovia and Bolam, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Mena-Segovia and Bolam, 2017).

claim: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons topographically innervate the striatum and striatal-projecting thalamic and midbrain dopamine neurons.
source: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons topographically innervate the striatum and striatal-projecting thalamic and midbrain dopamine neurons (Dautan et al., 2014), such that rostral PPN modulates motor-related circuits, LDT innervates limbic circuits, and caudal PPN targets both regions (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016) via both direct and indirect inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dautan et al., 2014; Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: Rostral PPN modulates motor-related circuits.
source: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons topographically innervate the striatum and striatal-projecting thalamic and midbrain dopamine neurons (Dautan et al., 2014), such that rostral PPN modulates motor-related circuits, LDT innervates limbic circuits, and caudal PPN targets both regions (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016) via both direct and indirect inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: LDT innervates limbic circuits.
source: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons topographically innervate the striatum and striatal-projecting thalamic and midbrain dopamine neurons (Dautan et al., 2014), such that rostral PPN modulates motor-related circuits, LDT innervates limbic circuits, and caudal PPN targets both regions (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016) via both direct and indirect inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: Caudal PPN targets both motor-related and limbic circuits.
source: PPN and LDT cholinergic neurons topographically innervate the striatum and striatal-projecting thalamic and midbrain dopamine neurons (Dautan et al., 2014), such that rostral PPN modulates motor-related circuits, LDT innervates limbic circuits, and caudal PPN targets both regions (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016) via both direct and indirect inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mena-Segovia, 2016; Xiao et al., 2016).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PPN cholinergic neurons alters locomotion speed.
source: Consistent with a central role in modulating locomotor activity, optogenetic stimulation of PPN cholinergic neurons alters locomotion speed, while stimulation of adjacent glutamatergic neurons induces locomotion (Xiao et al., 2016; Roseberry et al., 2016; Capelli et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Xiao et al., 2016; Roseberry et al., 2016; Capelli et al., 2017).

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PPN glutamatergic neurons induces locomotion.
source: Consistent with a central role in modulating locomotor activity, optogenetic stimulation of PPN cholinergic neurons alters locomotion speed, while stimulation of adjacent glutamatergic neurons induces locomotion (Xiao et al., 2016; Roseberry et al., 2016; Capelli et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Xiao et al., 2016; Roseberry et al., 2016; Capelli et al., 2017).

claim: Cholinergic PPN lesion alone or in combination with dopaminergic denervation impairs gait and causes postural abnormalities in primates.
source: Cholinergic PPN lesion alone or in combination with dopaminergic denervation impairs gait and causes postural abnormalities in primates (Grabli et al., 2013; Karachi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Grabli et al., 2013; Karachi et al., 2010).

claim: Cholinergic-selective PPN lesion impairs performance on the accelerating rotarod in rodents.
source: In rodents, cholinergic-selective PPN lesion impairs performance on the accelerating rotarod and alters sensorimotor gating (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b), while non-specific PPN ablation alters gait (Blanco-Lezcano et al., 2017) and impairs reversal learning (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b).

claim: Cholinergic-selective PPN lesion alters sensorimotor gating in rodents.
source: In rodents, cholinergic-selective PPN lesion impairs performance on the accelerating rotarod and alters sensorimotor gating (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b), while non-specific PPN ablation alters gait (Blanco-Lezcano et al., 2017) and impairs reversal learning (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b).

claim: Non-specific PPN ablation alters gait in rodents.
source: In rodents, cholinergic-selective PPN lesion impairs performance on the accelerating rotarod and alters sensorimotor gating (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b), while non-specific PPN ablation alters gait (Blanco-Lezcano et al., 2017) and impairs reversal learning (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Blanco-Lezcano et al., 2017).

claim: Non-specific PPN ablation impairs reversal learning in rodents.
source: In rodents, cholinergic-selective PPN lesion impairs performance on the accelerating rotarod and alters sensorimotor gating (MacLaren et al., 2014a; MacLaren et al., 2014b), while non-specific PPN ablation alters gait (Blanco-Lezcano et al., 2017) and impairs reversal learning (Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Syed et al., 2016).

claim: PPN cholinergic loss is linked to gait abnormalities in Parkinson disease.
source: PPN cholinergic loss is linked to gait abnormalities in Parkinson disease (Karachi et al., 2010; Bohnen et al., 2009), and brainstem lesions (including PPN loss) can result in complex dystonia (Jankovic and Patel, 1983; LeDoux and Brady, 2003; Loher and Krauss, 2009; Zweig et al., 1988; Mente et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Karachi et al., 2010; Bohnen et al., 2009).

claim: Brainstem lesions (including PPN loss) can result in complex dystonia.
source: PPN cholinergic loss is linked to gait abnormalities in Parkinson disease (Karachi et al., 2010; Bohnen et al., 2009), and brainstem lesions (including PPN loss) can result in complex dystonia (Jankovic and Patel, 1983; LeDoux and Brady, 2003; Loher and Krauss, 2009; Zweig et al., 1988; Mente et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Jankovic and Patel, 1983; LeDoux and Brady, 2003; Loher and Krauss, 2009; Zweig et al., 1988; Mente et al., 2018).

claim: Most studies have failed to demonstrate neuronal inclusions or overt cell loss in the brainstem region of DYT1 dystonia postmortem samples.
source: Systematic cholinergic brainstem cell counts have not been performed in DYT1 dystonia postmortem samples; most studies have failed to demonstrate neuronal inclusions or overt cell loss in this region (Paudel et al., 2014; Pratt et al., 2016; McNaught et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Paudel et al., 2014; Pratt et al., 2016; McNaught et al., 2004).

claim: Motor behavior is severely disrupted in ChAT-CKO mice.
source: Motor behavior is severely disrupted in ChAT-CKO mice, but is distinct from the Dlx-CKO phenotype (Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Motor behavior in ChAT-CKO mice is distinct from the Dlx-CKO phenotype.
source: Motor behavior is severely disrupted in ChAT-CKO mice, but is distinct from the Dlx-CKO phenotype (Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of behavioral phenotypes in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: ChAT-CKO pups are initially indistinguishable from littermates.
source: ChAT-CKO pups are initially indistinguishable from littermates, but at approximately 4 weeks of age develop a hunched posture, have unkempt fur, and exhibit reduced responsiveness to handling (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on observational data described in the text and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At approximately 4 weeks of age, ChAT-CKO mice develop a hunched posture.
source: ChAT-CKO pups are initially indistinguishable from littermates, but at approximately 4 weeks of age develop a hunched posture, have unkempt fur, and exhibit reduced responsiveness to handling (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on observational data described in the text and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At approximately 4 weeks of age, ChAT-CKO mice have unkempt fur.
source: ChAT-CKO pups are initially indistinguishable from littermates, but at approximately 4 weeks of age develop a hunched posture, have unkempt fur, and exhibit reduced responsiveness to handling (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on observational data described in the text and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At approximately 4 weeks of age, ChAT-CKO mice exhibit reduced responsiveness to handling.
source: ChAT-CKO pups are initially indistinguishable from littermates, but at approximately 4 weeks of age develop a hunched posture, have unkempt fur, and exhibit reduced responsiveness to handling (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on observational data described in the text and shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit severe kyphosis, including during locomotion.
source: Whereas normal mice exhibit a slight dorsal spinal curvature at rest, ChAT-CKO mice exhibit severe kyphosis, including during locomotion (assessed by two observers blind to experimental conditions; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Figure 3—video 1) (Guyenet et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—video 1.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit a significantly reduced ability to hang by the forelimbs.
source: ChAT-CKO mice also exhibit signs of weakness, including a significantly reduced ability to hang by the forelimbs (Figure 3C), tremulous movements, labored breathing (Figure 3—video 1), and significantly reduced horizontal and vertical movement in the open field (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit tremulous movements.
source: ChAT-CKO mice also exhibit signs of weakness, including a significantly reduced ability to hang by the forelimbs (Figure 3C), tremulous movements, labored breathing (Figure 3—video 1), and significantly reduced horizontal and vertical movement in the open field (Figure 3D,E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3—video 1.

claim: ChAT-CKO mice exhibit labored breathing.
